stimuli.title: The Federalist No. 39 (1788): What Makes a Republic
stimuli.html:
If we resort for a criterion to the different principles on which different forms of government are established, we may define a republic to be, or at least may bestow that name on, a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior. It is ESSENTIAL to such a government that it be derived from the great body of the society, not from an inconsiderable proportion, or a favored class of it . . .

. . . The House of Representatives will derive its powers from the people of America . . . The Senate, on the other hand, will derive its powers from the States, as political and coequal societies . . .
stimuli.source: Excerpts from The Federalist No. 39, by James Madison (published under the pen name "Publius"), January 1788

stimuli.title: The Federalist No. 39 (1788): National or Federal?
stimuli.html:
In this essay, Madison used the word federal to describe a union of states in which the central government acts through the state governments. He used the word national to describe a government that acts directly on individual citizens.

. . . its jurisdiction extends to certain enumerated objects only, and leaves to the several States a residuary and inviolable sovereignty over all other objects. . . .

The proposed Constitution, therefore, is, in strictness, neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both. In its foundation it is federal, not national; in the sources from which the ordinary powers of the government are drawn, it is partly federal and partly national; in the operation of these powers, it is national, not federal; in the extent of them, again, it is federal, not national; and, finally, in the authoritative mode of introducing amendments, it is neither wholly federal nor wholly national.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from The Federalist No. 39, by James Madison, January 1788

stimuli.title: The Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964)
stimuli.html:
Section 1. The right of citizens . . . to vote in any primary or other election for President or Vice President, for electors for President or Vice President, or for Senator or Representative in Congress, shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or any State by reason of failure to pay any poll tax or other tax.

(Section 2 gives Congress the authority to pass laws carrying out this amendment.)

Background: A poll tax was a flat fee that a person had to pay before voting. After Reconstruction, several Southern states adopted poll taxes, along with other barriers, that kept many poor and Black citizens from the ballot box. By the early 1960s, only five states still charged a poll tax. Congress proposed the amendment in 1962, and the states ratified it in January 1964.
stimuli.source: Amendment XXIV, Constitution of the United States, ratified January 1964 (Section 1 excerpted; Section 2 summarized); background written for this test

stimuli.title: Opening the Ballot Box to Younger Voters
stimuli.html:
The Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971)

Section 1. The right of citizens of the United States, who are eighteen years of age or older, to vote shall not be denied or abridged . . . on account of age.

(Like the Twenty-fourth Amendment, Section 2 gives Congress the authority to pass laws carrying out this amendment.)

Background

For most of the nation's history, nearly every state set its voting age at 21. During the Vietnam War, however, young men could be drafted into the military at 18. Many Americans asked why citizens who were old enough to be sent to war were not old enough to vote. In 1970 Congress passed a law lowering the voting age to 18 for all elections. Later that year, in Oregon v. Mitchell, the Supreme Court ruled that Congress could set the voting age for federal elections but not for state and local elections. Many states now faced the expense and confusion of keeping two sets of voter lists. Congress proposed the Twenty-sixth Amendment in March 1971, and the states ratified it in just over three months, faster than any other amendment.
stimuli.source: Amendment XXVI, Constitution of the United States, ratified July 1971 (Section 1 excerpted; Section 2 summarized); background written for this test

stimuli.title: Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
stimuli.html:
Background: The state of New York gave Robert Livingston and Robert Fulton the sole right to run steamboats on the state's waters. Aaron Ogden held a license under this monopoly to carry passengers by steamboat between New York City and New Jersey. Thomas Gibbons ran competing steamboats on the same route. Gibbons held a federal license issued under a 1793 act of Congress that governed ships trading along the coast. New York courts ordered Gibbons to stop, and he appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the Court's opinion.

From the opinion:

The word "among" means intermingled with. . . . Commerce among the States cannot stop at the external boundary line of each State, but may be introduced into the interior. . . .

What is this power? It is the power to regulate, that is, to prescribe the rule by which commerce is to be governed. This power, like all others vested in Congress, is complete in itself, may be exercised to its utmost extent, and acknowledges no limitations other than are prescribed in the Constitution.

The Court concluded that New York's law, by keeping a federally licensed vessel off the state's waters, "comes, we think, in direct collision with that act" of Congress.
stimuli.source: Background written for this test; excerpts from the opinion of Chief Justice John Marshall, Gibbons v. Ogden, U.S. Supreme Court, 1824

stimuli.title: Letter to the Editor
stimuli.html:
To the Editor:

Sixteen-year-olds are mature enough to make serious decisions, so they should be allowed to vote in our city elections. Since the Twenty-sixth Amendment was ratified in 1971, no state may deny the vote to citizens 18 or older because of their age. Teenagers care more about the future of our parks and schools than most adults do. Letting young people vote early would build habits that last a lifetime. Anyone who opposes this idea simply does not trust young people. The city council should put this question on the ballot next year.

— A high school senior
stimuli.source: Original letter written for this test

stimuli.title: The Missouri Compromise (1820)
stimuli.html:
Background: In 1819, the Missouri Territory asked to join the Union as a state that allowed slavery. Northern members of Congress objected, and a bitter debate followed. Because each state has two senators, admitting Missouri as a slave state would have given slave states a majority in the Senate. In 1820, Congress reached a compromise. Maine, which had been part of Massachusetts, would enter the Union as a free state. Missouri would be allowed to enter as a slave state. Section 8 of the law also addressed the rest of the land the United States had bought from France in the Louisiana Purchase:

That in all that territory ceded by France to the United States, under the name of Louisiana, which lies north of thirty-six degrees and thirty minutes north latitude, not included within the limits of the state, contemplated by this act, slavery and involuntary servitude, otherwise than in the punishment of crimes, whereof the parties shall have been duly convicted, shall be, and is hereby, forever prohibited.
stimuli.source: Background written for this test; excerpt from Section 8, An Act to authorize the people of the Missouri territory to form a constitution and state government, March 6, 1820

stimuli.title: The New Nationalism (1910)
stimuli.html:
On August 31, 1910, former President Theodore Roosevelt spoke to a large crowd in Osawatomie, Kansas. He said:

I stand for the square deal. But when I say that I am for the square deal, I mean not merely that I stand for fair play under the present rules of the game, but that I stand for having those rules changed so as to work for a more substantial equality of opportunity and of reward for equally good service. . . .

The absence of effective State, and, especially, national, restraint upon unfair money-getting has tended to create a small class of enormously wealthy and economically powerful men, whose chief object is to hold and increase their power. . . .

The New Nationalism puts the national need before sectional or personal advantage. . . . This New Nationalism regards the executive power as the steward of the public welfare.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from Theodore Roosevelt's "New Nationalism" speech, Osawatomie, Kansas, August 31, 1910

stimuli.title: Remarks at the Brandenburg Gate (1987)
stimuli.html:
On June 12, 1987, President Ronald Reagan spoke in West Berlin, in front of the Brandenburg Gate and the Berlin Wall. He said:

Behind me stands a wall that encircles the free sectors of this city . . . Standing before the Brandenburg Gate, every man is a German, separated from his fellow men. Every man is a Berliner, forced to look upon a scar. . . .

In the 1950s, Khrushchev predicted: "We will bury you." But in the West today, we see a free world that has achieved a level of prosperity and well-being unprecedented in all human history. In the Communist world, we see failure, technological backwardness, declining standards of health, even want of the most basic kind—too little food. . . . Freedom leads to prosperity. . . .

General Secretary Gorbachev, if you seek peace, if you seek prosperity for the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, if you seek liberalization: Come here to this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!
stimuli.source: Excerpts from President Ronald Reagan's Remarks on East-West Relations at the Brandenburg Gate, West Berlin, June 12, 1987

items.prompt: According to Madison, which description fits a republic?
options: A government that gets its powers from the great body of the people and is run by officials who serve for limited terms or during good behavior
A government led by a single ruler who inherits power and serves for life
A government in which every citizen votes directly on every law
A government in which the states hold all power and the central government holds none
items.explain: Madison defines a republic as "a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior." A ruler who inherits power describes a monarchy. Citizens voting on every law describes a direct democracy; in a republic, the people choose representatives. Madison's definition says nothing about states holding all power.
why: A ruler who inherits power and serves for life describes a monarchy. Madison says a republic's officials serve “for a limited period, or during good behavior” and get power from the people.
Citizens voting on every law is a direct democracy. Madison's republic is “administered by persons holding their offices,” that is, representatives.
Madison's definition says nothing about states holding all power; it is about power coming from “the great body of the people.”

items.prompt: Madison writes that a republic must be derived "from the great body of the society, not from an inconsiderable proportion, or a favored class of it." Which kind of government is he rejecting?
options: A government based on popular sovereignty
A government controlled by a small, privileged group
A government with separate legislative, executive, and judicial branches
A government with an elected legislature
items.explain: "An inconsiderable proportion, or a favored class" means a small, privileged part of society, such as a wealthy elite or a hereditary nobility. Madison insists that a true republic cannot rest on such a group. Popular sovereignty (power coming from the people) and an elected legislature are exactly what he supports, not what he rejects. Separation of powers is not discussed in this excerpt.
why: Popular sovereignty means power comes from the people, which is exactly what Madison supports, not what he rejects.
Separation of powers is not discussed in this excerpt; Madison is rejecting rule by a small, favored group.
An elected legislature draws power from the people, which Madison supports; the House, he says, derives its powers “from the people of America.”

items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

Madison explains that the House of Representatives derives its powers from {{0}}, while the Senate derives its powers from {{1}}. Under the original Constitution, this is why senators were chosen by {{2}}.

options: the people of America
the States
the President
the Supreme Court
why: The excerpt says the Senate, not the House, derives its powers “from the States.”
The excerpt does not tie the House to the President; it says the House derives its powers “from the people of America.”
The Supreme Court is not a source of the House's power; the excerpt names the people.

options: the people of America
the States
the President
the Supreme Court
why: The excerpt says the House, not the Senate, derives its powers from the people.
The excerpt says the Senate derives its powers from the States, not from the President.
The Supreme Court is not mentioned as a source of the Senate's power; the excerpt names the States.

options: the voters of each state
the legislature of each state
the Electoral College
the House of Representatives
why: Direct election of senators by voters came only with the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913, not under the original Constitution.
The Electoral College chooses the President, not senators.
The House of Representatives never chose senators; under the original Constitution, each state legislature did.

items.explain: The excerpt states, "The House of Representatives will derive its powers from the people of America" and "The Senate, on the other hand, will derive its powers from the States." Because the Senate represented the states as "political and coequal societies," the original Constitution had each state legislature choose its senators (two per state, whatever its population). Voters did not elect senators directly until the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913. The Electoral College chooses the President, not senators.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the excerpt?
options: The Constitution creates a purely national government that replaces the states.
The Constitution leaves the states fully in control, just as the Articles of Confederation did.
The Constitution combines features of a national government and a federal union of states.
The Constitution can be amended only by the national government.
items.explain: Madison concludes that the Constitution "is, in strictness, neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both." He then shows which parts are federal, which are national, and which are mixed. A purely national government that replaces the states and a union that leaves the states fully in control each describe only one side. The claim that only the national government can amend the Constitution is wrong because Madison says the amendment process is "neither wholly federal nor wholly national"; amendments must be ratified by the states.
why: Madison says the Constitution is “neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both,” so it does not replace the states.
This describes only the federal side. Madison says that in the operation of its powers the Constitution is “national, not federal.”
Madison says the amendment process is “neither wholly federal nor wholly national”; amendments must be ratified by the states.

items.prompt: Madison writes that "in the operation of these powers, it is national, not federal." Which feature of the Constitution best illustrates this point?
options: Each state has two senators, no matter how large its population is.
The Constitution was ratified by a separate convention in each state.
Amendments must be ratified by three-fourths of the states.
The national government can collect taxes directly from individual citizens.
items.explain: The excerpt defines "national" as a government that acts directly on individual citizens. Collecting taxes directly from individuals is the national government acting on people without going through state governments. (Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could only ask the states for money.) Equal representation of states in the Senate, ratification by state conventions, and ratification of amendments by the states are all examples of the states acting as members of a union, which Madison calls "federal."
why: Equal state representation in the Senate treats the states as members of a union, which Madison calls “federal,” not national.
Ratification by state conventions shows the federal foundation; Madison says “in its foundation it is federal.”
Ratification of amendments by the states is a federal feature, not an example of the government acting directly on individuals.

items.prompt: Madison says the national government's jurisdiction "extends to certain enumerated objects only, and leaves to the several States a residuary and inviolable sovereignty over all other objects." Which part of the Constitution most directly puts this idea into writing?
options: The Tenth Amendment, which reserves powers not delegated to the United States to the states or the people
The First Amendment, which protects freedom of speech and religion
The Twenty-sixth Amendment, which protects the right of 18-year-olds to vote
The Preamble, which lists the goals of the Constitution
items.explain: "Enumerated objects" are the listed powers of the national government, and "residuary . . . sovereignty over all other objects" means the states keep the remaining powers. The Tenth Amendment says this directly: powers not delegated to the United States, nor prohibited to the states, "are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." The First and Twenty-sixth Amendments protect individual rights, and the Preamble states goals rather than dividing power.
why: The First Amendment protects individual rights such as speech and religion; it does not divide power between the nation and the states.
The Twenty-sixth Amendment protects 18-year-olds' right to vote; it does not reserve powers to the states.
The Preamble lists the Constitution's goals; it does not divide powers between the national government and the states.

items.prompt: Based on the table, sort each office according to how it is filled today.
bins: Not elected directly by the voters
items.explain: Elected directly: Representatives have always been elected by the voters, and senators have been elected directly by the voters since the Seventeenth Amendment (1913). Not elected directly: the President and Vice President are formally chosen by electors (the Electoral College), even though the voters' choices in each state determine which electors are selected; Supreme Court justices are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate. A common mistake is placing senators in the second group because of how they were chosen in 1789.
items.why: The most common mistake is placing U.S. Senator under Not elected directly because senators were chosen by state legislatures in 1789. The question asks about today: since the Seventeenth Amendment (1913), voters elect senators directly.

items.prompt: What did the Twenty-fourth Amendment accomplish?
options: It lowered the voting age in federal elections to 18.
It barred the United States and the states from denying citizens the vote in federal elections because they did not pay a poll tax or other tax.
It protected the right of women to vote in all elections.
It required every state to hold primary elections for President.
items.explain: Section 1 says the right to vote in elections for President, Vice President, presidential electors, senators, and representatives "shall not be denied or abridged . . . by reason of failure to pay any poll tax or other tax." Lowering the voting age was the Twenty-sixth Amendment, and women's voting rights were protected by the Nineteenth Amendment. The amendment mentions primaries but does not require states to hold them.
why: Lowering the voting age to 18 was the Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971), not the Twenty-fourth.
Women's right to vote was protected by the Nineteenth Amendment (1920).
Section 1 mentions primaries only to protect voting in them; it does not require states to hold primaries.

items.prompt: Based only on the text of the Twenty-fourth Amendment, a poll tax in which election was the amendment not written to forbid?
options: A primary election for U.S. Senate
An election for presidential electors
An election for state governor
A general election for the U.S. House of Representatives
items.explain: The amendment lists only federal offices: President, Vice President, presidential electors, Senator, and Representative in Congress, including primaries for those offices. A governor is a state official, so the amendment's text does not cover that election. Two years later, in Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections (1966), the Supreme Court ruled that poll taxes in state elections violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Every other choice is named in Section 1.
why: Section 1 names “any primary or other election” for Senator, so a Senate primary is covered.
Section 1 names elections “for electors for President or Vice President,” so this election is covered.
Section 1 names elections for “Representative in Congress,” so a House general election is covered.

items.prompt: According to the background reading, which situation helped lead to the Twenty-sixth Amendment?
options: The Twenty-fourth Amendment had already lowered the voting age for federal elections to 18.
The Supreme Court had ruled that states could no longer set any age requirement for voting.
Most states had already lowered their voting age to 16.
Young men could be drafted at 18 to fight in the Vietnam War, even though most states did not let them vote until 21.
items.explain: The reading explains that "young men could be drafted into the military at 18" while nearly every state set its voting age at 21, and many Americans asked why people old enough to be sent to war could not vote. The confusion caused by Oregon v. Mitchell (two sets of voter lists) added pressure. The Twenty-fourth Amendment dealt with poll taxes, not age; the Court did not strike down all age requirements; and states had not lowered the age to 16.
why: The Twenty-fourth Amendment banned poll taxes in federal elections; it did not change the voting age.
Oregon v. Mitchell said Congress could set the age for federal elections but not state elections; it did not end all state age requirements.
The reading says nearly every state set its voting age at 21, not 16.

items.prompt: Compare the Twenty-fourth Amendment (shown earlier) with the Twenty-sixth Amendment. Which statements are true of both amendments? Select two answers.
options: Both forbid the United States and the states from denying the vote for the reason the amendment names.
Both give Congress the power to enforce the amendment through appropriate laws.
Both apply only to elections for federal offices.
Both were ratified in the years right after the Civil War.
Both require citizens to pay a fee before they may vote.
items.explain: Section 1 of each amendment says the right to vote "shall not be denied or abridged" by the United States or by any state for a named reason (failure to pay a tax; age, for citizens 18 or older), and Section 2 of each gives Congress the authority to pass laws enforcing it. Only the Twenty-fourth is limited to federal elections; the Twenty-sixth covers all elections. They were ratified in 1964 and 1971, not after the Civil War, and both expand voting rather than requiring a fee.
why: Only the Twenty-fourth is limited to federal elections; the Twenty-sixth covers all elections.
The amendments were ratified in 1964 and 1971, about a century after the Civil War.
Both amendments expand voting; the Twenty-fourth actually bans requiring a tax to vote.

items.prompt: Marshall writes that "commerce among the States cannot stop at the external boundary line of each State, but may be introduced into the interior." Which conclusion does this statement support?
options: Congress may regulate trade and travel that crosses state lines, even when it moves through waters inside a state.
Each state may decide for itself whether ships from other states may enter its waters.
Congress may regulate only trade that takes place entirely inside a single state.
Commerce includes only the buying and selling of goods, not the transportation of passengers.
items.explain: Marshall's point is that the power to regulate commerce "among the States" does not end at a state's border; it reaches into a state wherever interstate commerce goes. Steamboats carrying passengers between New York and New Jersey were part of that commerce, so Congress's power covered them. The idea that each state may decide for itself whether ships from other states may enter its waters is the position New York took and the Court rejected. Marshall's reasoning concerns commerce among states, not commerce entirely within one state, and the case itself involved carrying passengers.
why: Letting each state decide was New York's position, which the Court rejected; Marshall says interstate commerce does not stop at a state's border.
Marshall's statement is about commerce “among the States,” trade that crosses state lines, not trade entirely within one state.
The case itself involved steamboats carrying passengers, and the Court treated that as commerce.

items.prompt: What was the most likely effect of the Supreme Court's decision in Gibbons v. Ogden?
options: States gained the power to grant monopolies over routes between states.
Steamboat operators with federal licenses could compete on routes between states, and national power over interstate commerce grew.
Congress lost its power to license ships that traded along the coast.
The Court declared the commerce power unconstitutional.
items.explain: The Court ruled that New York's monopoly law conflicted with the federal licensing act, so the monopoly could not keep federally licensed boats like Gibbons's off the route. This opened steamboat travel to competition and established that Congress's power over interstate commerce is "complete in itself." The decision did the opposite of giving states monopoly power, and it upheld rather than weakened Congress's licensing and commerce powers.
why: The decision struck down New York's monopoly on an interstate route, so states did not gain this power.
The Court upheld the federal licensing act; Congress kept its power to license coastal ships.
The Court upheld the commerce power, calling it “complete in itself.”

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of {{0}}, holding that New York's monopoly law could not be enforced against a vessel with a federal license. When a valid federal law and a state law conflict, the federal law wins because of {{1}}.

the state of New York
why: Ogden's claim depended on New York's monopoly, which the Court found in “direct collision” with federal law, so Ogden lost.

options: the Supremacy Clause
the First Amendment
the Tenth Amendment
the Twenty-fourth Amendment
why: The First Amendment protects speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition; it does not settle conflicts between federal and state laws.
The Tenth Amendment reserves powers to the states; it does not make state law win when Congress acts within its powers.
The Twenty-fourth Amendment bans poll taxes; it has nothing to do with conflicts between federal and state laws.

items.explain: Gibbons held the federal license, and the Court found that New York's law came "in direct collision" with the act of Congress, so the Court ruled for Gibbons. Ogden's claim depended on the New York monopoly, which lost. Article VI of the Constitution, the Supremacy Clause, makes the Constitution and federal laws made under it "the supreme Law of the Land," so a conflicting state law must give way. The Tenth Amendment reserves powers to the states; it does not settle conflicts in their favor when Congress acts within its powers.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the cartoonist's message?
options: Voters should register before Election Day so they do not lose their chance to vote.
Wealthy citizens should not be allowed to vote in federal elections.
Charging a tax to vote turns a basic right of citizenship into something only people with money can use.
Polling places should collect taxes so that elections pay for themselves.
items.explain: The cartoon shows the well-dressed man paying and walking in while the worker, who is registered, is turned away because his pockets are empty. The ironic caption "Free Country. Admission Extra." criticizes treating voting like a paid ticket. This was the problem the Twenty-fourth Amendment addressed; poll taxes had been used, especially in the South, to keep poor and Black citizens from voting. The worker already holds a registration card, so registration is not the issue, and the cartoon does not argue for keeping wealthy people from voting.
why: The worker already holds a voter registration card, so registration is not the problem the cartoon shows.
The cartoon criticizes keeping poor people out, not letting wealthy people in; it does not argue for barring anyone.
The caption “Free Country. Admission Extra.” mocks charging to vote; the cartoonist opposes the tax, not supports it.

items.prompt: Only one sentence in the letter could be confirmed or disproved using reliable sources, because it reports a fact instead of the writer's judgment. Click that sentence.
spans: Sixteen-year-olds are mature enough to make serious decisions, so they should be allowed to vote in our city elections.
Since the Twenty-sixth Amendment was ratified in 1971, no state may deny the vote to citizens 18 or older because of their age.
Teenagers care more about the future of our parks and schools than most adults do.
Letting young people vote early would build habits that last a lifetime.
Anyone who opposes this idea simply does not trust young people.
The city council should put this question on the ballot next year.
items.explain: The ratification date and the content of the Twenty-sixth Amendment can be checked in the Constitution and in historical records, so that sentence is a fact. The other sentences are judgments or predictions: "mature enough," "care more . . . than most adults," "would build habits," "simply does not trust," and "should" all signal the writer's opinions. The sentence about lifelong habits sounds factual, but it is a prediction the letter offers no evidence for.
items.why: Many students click “Letting young people vote early would build habits that last a lifetime” because it sounds factual, but it is a prediction with no evidence. Only the sentence about the Twenty-sixth Amendment's 1971 ratification and its content can be checked in the Constitution and historical records.

items.prompt: The writer claims, "Letting young people vote early would build habits that last a lifetime." Which piece of evidence, if accurate, would best support this claim?
options: A survey showing that most 16-year-olds in the city have part-time jobs
A quotation from one 16-year-old who says she would like to vote
The fact that the voting age for federal elections is 18
A study finding that people who vote in the first election they are eligible for are more likely to keep voting in later elections
items.explain: The claim is about habits: voting early leads to voting for life. A study linking first-time voting to continued voting later directly tests that idea. Part-time jobs have nothing to do with voting habits. One person's wish to vote is a single anecdote about interest, not about lifelong habits. The federal voting age is a fact, but it does not show that early voting builds habits.
why: Part-time jobs have nothing to do with whether early voting builds lifelong voting habits.
One person's wish to vote is a single anecdote about interest, not evidence about lifelong habits.
The federal voting age is a fact, but it does not show that voting early builds habits.

items.prompt: Madison wrote that the Senate would "derive its powers from the States." Based on the table, which change made senators answer directly to the voters instead of to the state legislatures?
options: The Seventeenth Amendment (1913)
The Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964)
The Twenty-sixth Amendment (1971)
The decision in Gibbons v. Ogden (1824)
items.explain: The table shows that senators were originally "chosen by the legislature of each state" and are now "elected directly by the voters of each state (Seventeenth Amendment, 1913)." The Twenty-fourth and Twenty-sixth Amendments expanded who may vote but did not change how senators are chosen. Gibbons v. Ogden concerned the commerce power, not elections.
why: The Twenty-fourth Amendment banned poll taxes in federal elections; it did not change how senators are chosen.
The Twenty-sixth Amendment lowered the voting age to 18; it did not change how senators are chosen.
Gibbons v. Ogden concerned the commerce power, not elections.

items.prompt: What did Section 8 of the Missouri Compromise do?
options: It ended slavery in every state of the Union.
It banned slavery in the Louisiana Purchase lands north of 36°30′ north latitude, except in the new state of Missouri.
It allowed slavery in all of the Louisiana Purchase lands.
It allowed each new territory to vote on whether to permit slavery.
items.explain: Section 8 says that in the territory "ceded by France . . . under the name of Louisiana, which lies north of thirty-six degrees and thirty minutes north latitude, not included within the limits of the state" (Missouri), slavery "is hereby, forever prohibited." It did not affect existing states. Letting territories vote on slavery (popular sovereignty) came later, in the Compromise of 1850 and the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854; the Kansas-Nebraska Act repealed this line.
why: Section 8 applied only to Louisiana Purchase territory north of 36°30′; it did not affect existing states.
Section 8 did the opposite for the northern part, declaring slavery “forever prohibited” north of 36°30′.
Letting territories vote on slavery (popular sovereignty) came later, in 1850 and 1854; Section 8 drew a fixed line.

items.prompt: Based on the table, how many slave states were in the Union after Missouri was admitted in 1821?
items.explain:
At the end of 1815 there were 9 slave states. The table adds three more slave states: Mississippi (1817), Alabama (1819), and Missouri (1821).
9 + 3 = 12 slave states.
The free states also grew from 9 to 12 (Indiana, Illinois, Maine), so after 1821 the Union had 12 free and 12 slave states. A common error is counting only the states in the table (3) or answering 24, the total number of states.

mistakes.why: 3 counts only the slave states in the table. Add them to the 9 slave states at the end of 1815: 9 + 3 = 12.
24 is the total number of states (12 free and 12 slave). The question asks only for slave states: 12.
11 is the count before Missouri entered (9 + Mississippi + Alabama). Adding Missouri in 1821 makes 12.

items.prompt: Based on the reading and the table, why did Congress pair the admission of Maine with the admission of Missouri?
options: To give the free states a permanent majority in the House of Representatives
To reward Massachusetts for its support of the War of 1812
To keep the number of free states and slave states equal, preserving the balance in the Senate
To make sure that both new states would allow slavery
items.explain: Before the compromise there were 11 free and 11 slave states. Admitting Missouri alone as a slave state would have given the slave states a 12-to-11 edge and a majority in the Senate, where each state has two votes. Adding Maine as a free state kept the count even at 12 and 12. Representation in the House depends on population, not the number of states, and Maine entered as a free state, not a slave state.
why: House seats depend on population, not on the number of states, and the goal was balance, not a free-state majority.
The reading says nothing about rewarding Massachusetts; Maine was paired with Missouri to keep the Senate balanced.
Maine entered as a free state, not a slave state.

items.skill: History: main idea of a speech
items.prompt: When Roosevelt says he stands for "having those rules changed so as to work for a more substantial equality of opportunity," what is he arguing?
options: Government should stay out of the economy and let the market decide all outcomes.
State governments, not the national government, should handle all economic issues.
Wealthy business owners deserve more political power because of their success.
Government should actively change laws so that economic competition is fairer to ordinary people.
items.explain: Roosevelt says the "square deal" means more than "fair play under the present rules"; it means changing the rules to create "a more substantial equality of opportunity." He criticizes the lack of "national restraint upon unfair money-getting" and says the New Nationalism "puts the national need before sectional or personal advantage." This is the opposite of leaving the economy alone or leaving it to the states, and he criticizes the "small class of enormously wealthy and economically powerful men" rather than praising them.
why: Roosevelt wants rules changed and calls for “national restraint upon unfair money-getting,” the opposite of leaving the economy alone.
Roosevelt stresses “especially, national” restraint and puts “the national need before sectional” advantage, so he does not leave it all to the states.
Roosevelt criticizes the “small class of enormously wealthy and economically powerful men”; he does not want them to have more power.

items.prompt: Progressive Era reforms had two main goals: regulating business to protect the public, and giving citizens a greater voice in government. Sort each reform from the timeline into the goal it served.
bins: Regulating business to protect the public
Giving citizens a greater voice in government
items.explain: Regulating business: the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act set safety rules for food and medicine companies, and the Clayton Antitrust Act limited business practices that reduce competition. Greater voice in government: the Seventeenth Amendment let voters elect senators directly, and the Nineteenth Amendment protected women's right to vote. A common mistake is placing the Seventeenth Amendment under business regulation because it passed in a busy reform year; it changed how senators are chosen, not how businesses operate.
items.why: The most common mistake is placing the Seventeenth Amendment under business regulation because it came during the reform years. It let voters elect senators directly, which gives citizens a greater voice; the Pure Food and Drug, Meat Inspection, and Clayton Acts are the business rules.

items.prompt: Reagan claims that "Freedom leads to prosperity." Which statement from the speech does he offer as evidence for this claim?
options: "But in the West today, we see a free world that has achieved a level of prosperity and well-being unprecedented in all human history."
"Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!"
"Every man is a Berliner, forced to look upon a scar."
"Behind me stands a wall that encircles the free sectors of this city."
items.explain: Reagan supports his claim by contrasting the free West, which has reached prosperity "unprecedented in all human history," with the Communist world's "failure" and shortages. That comparison is his evidence. "Tear down this wall!" is a call to action, not evidence. The "scar" sentence is an emotional image of a divided city, and the sentence about the wall describes his setting; neither shows that freedom produces prosperity.
why: “Tear down this wall!” is a call to action, not evidence that freedom brings prosperity.
The “scar” sentence is an emotional image of a divided city; it does not show any link between freedom and prosperity.
This sentence describes the setting of the speech; it does not compare the prosperity of free and Communist countries.

items.prompt: Based on the timeline, about how long had the Berlin Wall been standing when Reagan gave his speech, and what happened about two and a half years after the speech?
options: About 26 years; the Soviet Union built the wall
About 26 years; East Germany opened the border crossings in the wall
About 42 years; East and West Germany reunited
About 16 years; the Berlin Airlift began
items.explain: The wall was built in 1961 and the speech was in 1987: 1987 − 1961 = 26 years. About two and a half years after June 1987 came November 1989, when East Germany opened the border crossings and crowds began tearing down the wall. The wall was built by East Germany in 1961, before the speech; reunification came in October 1990, more than three years after the speech; and the Airlift happened in 1948–1949, before the wall existed.
why: The 26 years is right, but East Germany built the wall in 1961, before the speech, not two and a half years after it.
42 years is the time since Germany was divided in 1945, not since the wall was built (1961). Reunification came more than three years after the speech.
1987 − 1961 = 26, not 16, and the Berlin Airlift happened in 1948–1949, long before the speech.

items.prompt: What happened to the value of the U.S. dollar compared with the tarv between 2021 and 2023?
options: It fell, because the number in the table went up.
It stayed the same, because the dollar is always worth one dollar.
It rose, because one dollar could be exchanged for more tarvs.
It fell, because one dollar could be exchanged for fewer tarvs.
items.explain: In 2021, one dollar bought 20 tarvs. In 2023, one dollar bought 30 tarvs. Because each dollar could be traded for more of the other currency, the dollar rose in value (strengthened) against the tarv. A common mistake is thinking a bigger number in the table means the dollar is weaker; here the number counts tarvs per dollar, so a bigger number means a stronger dollar. The dollar bought more tarvs, not fewer.
why: The table shows tarvs per dollar, so a bigger number means each dollar buys more tarvs: the dollar got stronger, not weaker.
The dollar's value compared with another currency can change; the exchange rate went from 20 to 30 tarvs per dollar.
The dollar bought more tarvs (30 in 2023 versus 20 in 2021), not fewer.

items.prompt: A guitar made in Tarvania sells for 6,000 tarvs. Using the 2023 exchange rate, what was the price of the guitar in U.S. dollars?
items.explain:
In 2023, 1 dollar = 30 tarvs.
Dollars = tarvs ÷ tarvs per dollar = 6,000 ÷ 30 = $200.
A common error is multiplying (6,000 × 30), which gives a far too large number, or using the 2021 rate (6,000 ÷ 20 = $300).

mistakes.why: You multiplied 6,000 by 30. To change tarvs into dollars, divide by the tarvs per dollar: 6,000 ÷ 30 = $200.
$300 uses the 2021 rate (20 tarvs per dollar). In 2023 the rate was 30: 6,000 ÷ 30 = $200.
$240 uses the 2024 rate (25 tarvs per dollar). The question asks for 2023: 6,000 ÷ 30 = $200.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

From 2023 to 2024, the U.S. dollar {{0}} against the tarv. As a result, goods imported from Tarvania became {{1}} for American buyers, and U.S. goods sold in Tarvania became {{2}} for Tarvanian buyers.

options: strengthened
weakened
did not change
why: The dollar bought 30 tarvs in 2023 but only 25 in 2024, so it weakened, not strengthened.
The rate changed from 30 to 25 tarvs per dollar, so the dollar's value did change.

options: less expensive
more expensive
no different in price
why: A weaker dollar buys fewer tarvs, so Tarvanian goods cost more dollars: the guitar went from $200 to $240.
The rate changed, so the dollar price changed: 6,000 tarvs cost $200 in 2023 and $240 in 2024.

options: less expensive
more expensive
no different in price
why: Each dollar is now worth fewer tarvs, so a U.S. product costs Tarvanians fewer tarvs: $100 went from 3,000 to 2,500 tarvs.
The rate changed, so the tarv price of U.S. goods changed too: from 3,000 to 2,500 tarvs for a $100 item.

items.explain: One dollar bought 30 tarvs in 2023 but only 25 tarvs in 2024, so the dollar weakened. The 6,000-tarv guitar cost 6,000 ÷ 30 = $200 in 2023 but 6,000 ÷ 25 = $240 in 2024, so Tarvanian imports became more expensive for Americans. A $100 U.S. product cost a Tarvanian buyer 100 × 30 = 3,000 tarvs in 2023 but only 100 × 25 = 2,500 tarvs in 2024, so U.S. goods became less expensive in Tarvania. A weaker dollar tends to help U.S. exporters and hurt U.S. buyers of imports.

items.prompt: Which statements are supported by the graph? Select two answers.
options: Country M had a trade surplus in 2023.
Country M's largest trade deficit in these years occurred in 2021.
Country M's exports increased every year from 2020 to 2024.
Country M's imports were greater than its exports in every year shown.
Country M's trade deficit in 2024 was larger than its trade deficit in 2022.
items.explain:
Exports minus imports for each year: 2020: 410 − 450 = −40; 2021: 395 − 480 = −85; 2022: 450 − 470 = −20; 2023: 470 − 465 = +5; 2024: 500 − 520 = −20.
2023 is the only surplus (+5), and 2021 has the largest deficit (85 billion). Exports fell from 2020 to 2021 (410 to 395), so they did not rise every year. Imports were not greater in 2023. The deficits in 2022 and 2024 were equal (20 billion each), so 2024's was not larger.
why: Exports fell from 410 to 395 billion between 2020 and 2021, so they did not rise every year.
In 2023, exports (470) were greater than imports (465), so imports were not greater every year.
The deficits in 2022 and 2024 were both 20 billion (450 − 470 and 500 − 520), so 2024's was not larger.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why Country M imports coffee, bananas, and cocoa?
options: Country M has a trade deficit, so it is required to import tropical crops.
Country M's farmers have chosen to stop growing all food crops.
Tropical crops cost less to ship than wheat and machinery.
Country M's climate is not suited to growing these crops, so it is more efficient to buy them from countries that can grow them.
items.explain: The reading says Country M has mild winters and cool summers, while coffee, bananas, and cocoa "grow only in hot, tropical climates." Differences in climate and resources lead countries to specialize in what they produce well (wheat, dairy, machinery) and trade for what they cannot produce efficiently. A trade deficit is a result of trade, not a rule that forces imports. Country M still grows wheat and dairy products, and the reading says nothing about shipping costs.
why: A trade deficit is a result of trading, not a rule that forces a country to import particular goods.
The reading says Country M exports wheat and dairy products, so its farmers still grow food.
The reading says nothing about shipping costs; it explains that these crops grow only in hot, tropical climates.

items.prompt: Based on the table, which region is best suited to large-scale grain farming?
options: Interior Plains
Rocky Mountains
Intermountain Region
Appalachian Mountains
items.explain: The Interior Plains have "flat to gently rolling land" with "deep, fertile soils," and the table lists "large-scale grain farming (corn and wheat)" as a common land use. The Rocky and Appalachian Mountains are too rugged for large fields, and the Intermountain Region gets "little rainfall," so farming there depends on irrigation.
why: The Rocky Mountains are “young, high, rugged,” used for mining, forestry, and tourism, not large grain fields.
The Intermountain Region gets “little rainfall,” so its farming depends on irrigation.
The Appalachian Mountains are used for coal mining and forestry; their land is too hilly for large-scale grain farming.

items.prompt: A traveler drives west across the United States, starting at the Atlantic Ocean and ending in Nevada. Drag each region into the order in which the traveler would cross it.
items.explain: Going east to west: (1) the Atlantic Coastal Plain along the ocean; (2) the Appalachian Mountains; (3) the Interior Plains, which lie "between the Appalachians and the Rockies"; (4) the Rocky Mountains; (5) the Intermountain Region, "between the Rockies and the Pacific mountain ranges," where Nevada's dry basins are. A common mistake is placing the Intermountain Region before the Rockies; the table says it lies west of them.
items.why: The most common mistake is placing the Intermountain Region before the Rocky Mountains. The table says it lies “between the Rockies and the Pacific mountain ranges,” so a westbound traveler crosses the Rockies first and reaches Nevada's dry basins last.

items.prompt: City B has much colder winters and hotter summers than City A. Which statement best explains this difference?
options: City B is closer to the equator than City A.
City B is far from the ocean, and land heats up and cools down faster than large bodies of water.
City B is at a much higher elevation than City A.
City B receives more sunlight in winter than City A.
items.explain: The cities are at the same latitude and elevation, so the key difference is distance from the ocean. Water heats and cools slowly, which keeps coastal City A mild all year (a range of 66 − 45 = 21°F). Inland City B has no such moderating effect, so it swings from 22°F in January to 77°F in July. Latitude and elevation are stated to be about the same, and more winter sunlight would make City B's winters warmer, not colder.
why: The reading says both cities are at about the same latitude, so distance from the equator does not explain the difference.
The reading says both cities are at about the same elevation.
More winter sunlight would make City B warmer in winter, but City B's winters are colder (22°F in January).

items.prompt: The annual temperature range is the difference between the warmest and coldest monthly averages. What is the annual temperature range for City B, in degrees Fahrenheit?
items.explain:
City B's warmest month is July (77°F) and its coldest month is January (22°F).
77 − 22 = 55°F.
A common error is using City A's values (66 − 45 = 21) or subtracting December (77 − 25 = 52), which is not the coldest month.

mistakes.why: 21 is City A's range (66 − 45). Use City B's values: 77 − 22 = 55.
You used December (25°F) as the coldest month. January is colder at 22°F: 77 − 22 = 55.
You used August (75°F) as the warmest month. July is warmer at 77°F: 77 − 22 = 55.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why Leeward Town receives so much less precipitation than Windward Town?
options: Leeward Town is closer to the ocean, so its air is drier.
Leeward Town is at a higher latitude, so it receives less sunlight to evaporate water.
Moist ocean air cools as it rises over the mountains and drops most of its moisture on the western slope, leaving dry air to descend on the eastern side.
Winds blow from east to west, carrying moisture away from Leeward Town toward the ocean.
items.explain: The prevailing winds carry moist air from the ocean toward the mountains. As the air is forced up the western slope, it cools, and the water vapor condenses into rain and snow, giving Windward Town about 63.6 inches a year. By the time the air crosses the crest and sinks down the eastern side, it has lost most of its moisture, so Leeward Town gets only about 9.2 inches. This dry zone is called a rain shadow. The reading says Windward Town faces the ocean and that winds blow from west to east, so the statements that Leeward Town is closer to the ocean and that winds blow from east to west both contradict it; nothing in the reading mentions a difference in latitude.
why: The reading says Windward Town faces the ocean, so Leeward Town is farther from it, not closer.
The reading never mentions a difference in latitude; the difference comes from the mountains.
The reading says the prevailing winds blow from west to east, from the ocean toward the land.
